Source evidence: La juge fédérale américaine Rita Lin a déclaré illégales, jeudi 27 août, les sanctions prises en février par l’administration Trump contre Anthropic, estimant que le gouvernement avait puni l’entreprise d’intelligence artificielle (IA) pour avoir critiqué publiquement le Pentagone, et non pas en raison de risques supposés.

« L’invocation creuse de la sécurité nationale n’est pas un chèque en blanc pour punir ceux qui critiquent le gouvernement », écrit la magistrate de San Francisco (Californie) dans une décision de 59 pages consultée par l’Agence France-Presse (AFP).

La juge Lin interdit à toutes les entités de l’exécutif et ministères de rompre leurs contrats avec Anthropic, comme leur avait enjoint Donald Trump en février. Le conflit avait éclaté après le refus de l’entreprise de lever certaines restrictions à l’utilisation de son modèle d’IA, Claude, pour des attaques létales entièrement autonomes ou la surveillance de masse des Américains. Donald Trump avait alors fustigé une entreprise de « la gauche radicale » et « hors de contrôle ».

Pas de menace réelle

Outre l’annulation de tous ses contrats, le ministère de la défense avait inscrit Anthropic sur la liste des entreprises présentant un « risque pour la chaîne d’approvisionnement » et la sécurité nationale, un statut jusque-là réservé à des entreprises étrangères. Cette désignation interdisait, de fait, à tous les prestataires du Pentagone d’utiliser les produits d’Anthropic dans le cadre de leur collaboration avec le ministère. L’épisode avait suscité l’émoi et fait craindre, un temps, pour l’avenir d’Anthropic.

La décision de jeudi rend permanente la suspension provisoire des sanctions ordonnée en mars par la juge et s’applique immédiatement. Le gouvernement peut faire appel.

Pour la juge fédérale, les mesures visaient à « faire un exemple » d’une entreprise jugée « arrogante », et non à parer à une menace réelle. Elle a relevé que le gouvernement avait abandonné en cours de procédure sa thèse selon laquelle Anthropic pouvait modifier après livraison ses modèles et les rendre potentiellement inopérants par l’armée. L’administration Trump s’est contentée d’invoquer une perte de « confiance » compte tenu des critiques publiques de l’entreprise.

« Nous restons concentrés sur une collaboration productive avec le gouvernement pour mettre l’IA au service de notre sécurité nationale, afin que tous les Américains bénéficient de cette technologie », a déclaré, de son côté, un porte-parole d’Anthropic à l’AFP.

Maintien des relations

La victoire d’Anthropic n’est toutefois pas totale, car cette décision ne concerne qu’une des deux procédures engagées par l’entreprise contre le gouvernement américain. La mise à l’écart de l’entreprise est aussi appuyée sur un texte du code des marchés publics fédéraux non examiné en Californie, et reste donc dans l’attente d’une décision d’un tribunal de Washington. Ce dernier a refusé en avril de suspendre la sanction.

Avant le jugement rendu jeudi, les relations entre la perle de l’IA et l’exécutif américain n’étaient cependant pas rompues. Le ministère de la défense continue de se servir des modèles d’Anthropic, les seuls habilités pour les opérations classifiées, même s’il a annoncé une transition progressive et a conclu, au début du mois de mai, des accords en ce sens avec tous les grands rivaux de la start-up.

Par ailleurs, Anthropic a donné accès au gouvernement Trump à son modèle le plus avancé, Mythos, jusqu’ici proposé uniquement à une poignée d’entreprises et organisations afin de renforcer leur sécurité informatique.

Rien de l’approche du gouvernement « ne cadre avec une crainte authentique vis-à-vis d’Anthropic, qui serait un saboteur prêt à empoisonner son logiciel pour compromettre la sécurité nationale », a estimé la juge Lin.

Critiqué par certains dans la Silicon Valley et au-delà, accusé de vouloir dicter ses conditions à l’exécutif, le patron d’Anthropic, Dario Amodei, s’en est défendu, mais n’est pas revenu sur sa position concernant l’emploi de sa technologie. « Cela ne vaut pas le coup de voir les démocraties triompher si elles utilisent ces moyens », a-t-il déclaré dans une interview à l’agence Bloomberg en juin, en référence à la surveillance par un pays de sa population et le recours à des attaques mortelles décidées par l’IA.

Pour lui, la saga politique, économique et judiciaire avec le ministère de la défense « a permis d’attirer l’attention sur ces sujets ».

Source evidence: Pope Leo XIV warned on Friday of the difficulty states face in overseeing artificial intelligence, which in his view is concentrated in the hands of a small number of major economic and technological players, and called for the use of such tools to be governed by ethical criteria.

“It is important that a certain ethics be established to accompany the use of these important tools which, unfortunately, are concentrated in the hands of major economic and technological players, and which the state finds it hard to control,” he said during an audience in the Clementine Hall of the Apostolic Palace with members of the Institut International des Sciences Administratives, a Brussels-based body, at the close of its annual conference held in Rome.

The pontiff called for acting so that “the good of the human family is not sacrificed to private interests,” and raised a question about the pace of technological development: “The speed at which innovations relating to artificial intelligence are developing leads us to ask whether in future it will be possible to control these machines, whether humanity does not risk becoming the victim of its own inventions.” He added that one of the grave problems of the present is seeing that “decisions about human life are entrusted to machines.”

Leo XIV defended what he called the irreplaceable character of human intelligence in the face of these tools and argued that the work of experts can help authorities take decisions in the field. He closed by encouraging participants to work towards the humanisation of digital technologies, “so that they serve life and peace.”

The address draws on Magnifica humanitas, the encyclical the Pope devoted to safeguarding the human person in the age of artificial intelligence, and comes a week after another audience on the same subject. On August 21, before some two hundred members of the International Catholic Legislators Network gathered in Rome, he warned of the risk that technological innovation could become “another instrument of ideological or economic colonialism,” a “subtle form of domination” capable of increasing poorer nations' dependence on richer ones.

On that occasion he argued that every technological achievement poses a moral question that is not confined to “what we can do, but what we should do,” and cautioned against the temptation to build “a new Tower of Babel where power, efficiency and control obscure the face of the human person.”

Artificial intelligence has been a central concern of the pontificate from its outset. Leo XIV, the first pope born in the United States, also holds Peruvian nationality after decades as a missionary and bishop of Chiclayo. He did not name any specific company.

Source evidence: University of Alberta Study Finds 87% of Canadian Musicians View Generative AI ‘Negatively’

The Western Canadian university surveyed 263 Canadian musicians about their thoughts on AI’s rampant rise and the use of streaming services as an artistic tool.

A new study from the University of Alberta surveyed 263 “working Canadian musicians,” asking them about their experiences working in the evolving music industry. As respondents discussed an increase in the industry’s tech advancements, namely generative AI, many were not optimistic.

Of the 142 participants who highlighted the rapid use of AI, 87% viewed it “negatively.” Many shared they are actively avoiding the tool in their music, with some explaining that it’s devaluing human-made work. As AI continues to affect the music industry, participants say that it’s becoming a challenge to bring in new listeners and earn a livable wage.

Beyond the moral implications of using AI, which the survey explains as “the loss of human artistry,” the surveyed musicians cited copyright theft, environmental concerns and the “fear that AI-generated tracks are drowning out authentic music, potentially threatening livelihoods.”

The use of AI in music is becoming one of the most talked-about issues within the community in Canada. Recently, there’s been a wave of artists' musical likeness being used to create AI music, and they have no clue and aren’t being compensated. Canadian singer Alessia Cara said it was "a little scary" after an AI-generated song appeared online. Meanwhile, The Atlantic reported that artists including Drake and The Weeknd, among others, were included in "four giant datasets of songs” being shared in the AI music development community.

It has even impacted the charts. “I Run” was a viral EDM track that debuted on the Billboard Canadian Hot 100, released by electronic duo HAVEN. After revealing that they had used the AI tool Suno to craft the uncredited female vocalist in the song — bearing similarities to Jorja Smith — the pair tapped TikTok singer Kaitlin Aragon to step in. This became the version that charted. In the U.S., rapper Fenix Flexin's '80s-sounding "Rubberz" charted on the Billboard Hot 100. After early denials, he admitted he used AI for the song.

This week, Billboard Canada joined Billboard in its affirmation towards transparency on the charts and in editorial when it comes to AI in music.

Others in the Canadian industry are approaching AI with optimism, finding ways to regulate it so human creators are still compensated and credited. Last year, it was announced that three major North American music rights organizations, including SOCAN, would accept registrations of partially-generated AI music while remaining vocal about the need for strict copyright laws to stop the theft of copyright-protected music in Canada, calling on the federal government to “enact meaningful input transparency laws.” SOCAN partnered with Musical AI last month to offer “consent management and attribution” for generative AI music being created, which CEO Jennifer Brown says the collaboration will establish “a foundation for attribution and compensation, to ensure that music creators are paid when their music is used by AI.”

Margaret McGuffin, CEO of Music Publishers Canada, was recognized as this year’s Impact Award recipient at Billboard Canada Power Players for her advocacy on the subject. Recently, the organization filed a submission with the federal court to intervene in one of the country’s first-ever legal proceedings on the role of generative AI in copyright laws. Depending on the outcome, the law could impact how the federal government determines whether an AI-assisted piece of music is eligible for copyright protection and set a precedent for who the rightful author of that work is.

In the digital age, it’s considered “a practical necessity” for success. However, participants shared there’s a “distrust over low payouts” and “opaque algorithms replacing organic discovery,” with many citing that the industry is “overly reliant on Spotify metrics to evaluate musicians” and “many wanted to leave these platforms but did not see any alternatives.”

“Musicians felt the shift to streaming about 10 years ago, and haven’t recovered or seen the benefits,” says the study’s lead researcher, Brian Fauteux, explaining that artists are facing “this other variable, AI, that is coming from the big tech world, from people who don’t seem interested in music as an art or a craft.”

Still, some artists have taken their music off the streaming platform. Throughout much of last year, artists including Chad VanGaalen, Sunnsetter, Deerhoof, Godspeed You! Black Emperor and Sarah Harmer removed their discographies from Spotify after news of CEO Daniel Ek's investment in an AI weapons company came to light. Ek has since stepped down from that role, but remains at the company.

Other Canadian artists have faced a rampant issue on Spotify: AI-generated music being uploaded to their profiles without their consent. Last July, singer-songwriter Leith Ross had eight AI-generated songs uploaded to their Spotify profile. Icon Anne Murray faced a similar situation at the top of the year, after four songs featuring a noticeably different voice appeared on the Canadian music legend's page.

“It’s not like this fell from the sky and people are mad about it,” Fauteux explains. “These problems go back to the years of record labels and exploitation, where you have many stories of musicians not being paid properly or having their rights stolen.”

Source 1
Publisher: EL PAÍS English
Date: 2026-08-29T04:00:00+00:00
Original headline: Charts that explain the rise of artificial intelligence
English normalization: Charts that explain the rise of artificial intelligence
Evidence basis: full_text
Source evidence: In just four years, artificial intelligence has emerged onto the world stage and transformed it. In the autumn of 2022, ChatGPT went viral: it made amusing mistakes and yet still gave the impression that something momentous was happening. Machines could now converse and understand human instructions. Their limits remain to be seen, but their impact on the economy and on everyday life is already clear. The following charts trace that rapid rise.

Models keep getting better

Chatbots from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google improve with every new release. To measure their progress, the industry has developed a series of competency tests known as benchmarks, and the results point to steady gains over time.

In 2023, the leading model of the day, GPT-4, scored 36% on GPQA, a benchmark designed to test doctoral-level scientific knowledge, well below the roughly 65% that PhD holders achieve in their own fields. Today, the best models are approaching 95%, pushing the benchmark to its limits as a measure of progress. The same pattern has been seen in coding and mathematics benchmarks. That is why new evaluations are constantly being developed, including variants of ARC-AGI, which are designed to pose problems that are easy for humans but difficult for machines. And, time and again, AI systems eventually learn to solve them.

Adoption has been massive: hundreds of millions of people use AI

Generative AI is likely the fastest-adopted mass technology in history. Personal computers took more than a decade to reach half of Americans. The internet took six years; the smartphone, five. Chatbots like ChatGPT or Gemini did it in just over two. In Spain, 55% of internet users say they already use generative AI tools, according to the Spanish National Observatory for Telecommunications and the Information Society (ONTSI).

This speed also reflects an increasingly digitalized world, and therefore a faster-moving one. Getting online once required installing a modem, and getting a cellphone meant going to a store. AI models, by contrast, are just software: a single click is enough to bring them into your home. Many of the technologies that follow are likely to spread just as quickly.

Equally, if not more important, is adoption by businesses. According to data from Ramp, which processes payments for tens of thousands of U.S. companies, more than half of businesses already pay for AI services from at least one provider. Forty-three percent pay for Anthropic’s Claude, which overtook OpenAI’s ChatGPT (40%) in professional settings a few months ago. In Spain, the trend is similar: according to ONTSI, 20% of medium-sized companies and 58% of large companies were using AI in 2025.

AI companies have seen their expectations and their market valuations soar

The world’s five most valuable companies are all technology firms: Nvidia, Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, and each has a major stake in artificial intelligence. Since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, Microsoft’s market value has doubled, Amazon’s has tripled, and Alphabet’s has nearly quadrupled.

Above all stands Nvidia, which went from making graphics cards for video games to powering the computation behind these models with hardware and software that are close to monopolistic. Since late 2022, its market value has increased fifteenfold. Its rise is hard to fathom: if you had invested $1,000 in the company in January 2010, that stake would be worth more than $600,000 today. It is little surprise that thousands of Nvidia employees have become millionaires.

The rest of the semiconductor supply chain has also enjoyed spectacular gains. Broadcom, which designs custom chips, is worth six times more than it was at the end of 2021. SK Hynix and Micron, which manufacture the memory used in AI chips, are worth 10 times more. And Dutch company ASML, whose machines are essential to the production of advanced semiconductors, has seen its value double.

Tech giants are investing like never before

This stock market boom has naturally raised concerns that a bubble may be forming. Even when a technology proves transformative, the companies betting on it can still fail if they arrive too early or back the wrong approach. That is one of the key lessons of the dot-com bubble and other speculative manias before it. The debate remains unresolved, but tech giants have shown no sign of slowing their spending: combined capital expenditures by Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta have quadrupled since 2023.

The boom is showing up in job postings

Many of AI’s effects on the labor market are still unknown. Will jobs be automated? How much will occupations change, and in what ways? Will the impact fall most heavily on young workers or on knowledge workers? These questions are still the subject of intense debate. But one consequence is already clear, and hardly surprising: job postings that mention AI have multiplied across countries such as the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom.

The cloud is more physical than it seems

Training and running AI models requires an extraordinary amount of computing power: vast data centers packed with millions of processors, first to train the models and then to handle the requests of individual users. Forecasts suggest that computing demand will continue to grow rapidly, even as models become more efficient.

And that growth carries an increasingly tangible physical cost. Land is needed to build data centers, silicon to make their chips, factories to produce their components, and electricity to keep the machines running around the clock. According to the International Energy Agency, electricity consumption by data centers is expected to more than double by 2030, rising from 415 to 945 terawatt-hours and approaching 3% of global electricity demand. That would be more electricity than Japan consumes in an entire year.

The United States still leads, but China remains only months behind

The most advanced AI models are still being developed by U.S. labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. But the gap with China has remained remarkably narrow, with Chinese companies typically matching leading U.S. models within a matter of months. According to the capabilities index compiled by Epoch AI, the top U.S. model scores 162 points (Claude Fable 5), while the leading Chinese model, Moonshot, has already reached 157.

In other words, China’s best model is now operating at roughly the same level as the leading U.S. model was earlier this year. Europe lags somewhat further behind: the top model from France’s Mistral scores 143 points. The race also highlights another divide. Many Chinese models are open weight, meaning they can be downloaded and run by anyone with a computer.

Using AI is getting cheaper

As models have improved, costs have fallen very quickly. Using the model behind the original version of ChatGPT cost around $20 per million tokens. Two years later, matching that level of performance with Llama, Meta’s open-weight model, cost just 10 cents, a 200-fold reduction.

According to estimates by Epoch AI, the cost of achieving a given level of capability falls by a factor of between ten and a thousand with each passing year. That is another reason for AI’s rapid rise: what is expensive and exclusive today is likely to become cheap and ubiquitous tomorrow.

What do we think about AI? Somewhere between enthusiasm and anxiety

The arrival of AI is likely to have social consequences across many areas of life. Its effects on education, the attention economy, artistic creation and cybersecurity are all being debated. This spring, Ipsos surveyed thousands of people in around 30 countries, asking whether AI-powered products “excite” them and whether they “make them nervous.” Spaniards feel both: 47% say they are excited by them, while 52% say they make them nervous.

The survey also points to a cultural divide. Although excitement and anxiety coexist in every country, often within the same person, anxiety tends to dominate in the West while excitement is more prevalent in Asia. Eighty-three percent of Chinese respondents and 79% of Indians say they are excited about AI, compared with 26% of Canadians and 33% of Americans. It will be interesting to revisit that question in three, five or 25 years.

Source evidence: Timothy Garton Ash is right that serious artificial intelligence risks demand international action, but “AI Hiroshima” may be the wrong picture (Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not, 22 August). Hiroshima was not technology going rogue. Human beings designed the bomb, authorised its use and dropped it. The technology worked much as intended.

AI may one day behave in ways we cannot control, but many of the gravest harms could happen without any dramatic moment when “the AI takes over”. AI might help design a pathogen, find a vulnerability in critical infrastructure or improve a weapons system while people still decide what happens next. Other harms may build almost invisibly through thousands of ordinary decisions – more autonomy here, one safeguard removed there, another consequential task handed over because the system has worked well so far. By the time the danger is obvious, the important decisions may already have been made.

That is also where international agreement could begin. We do not need countries to agree about superintelligence or the probability of human extinction before agreeing that there are some doors AI should never be allowed to open by itself. Weapons systems, critical infrastructure and biological synthesis are obvious places to start. Governments could agree minimum safeguards, require clear human authority for the most consequential actions, keep records of who authorised what and share serious failures and near-misses internationally.

The greatest AI dangers may not arrive with a mushroom cloud. They may arrive quietly, one apparently reasonable step at a time. If we want effective AI governance, we need to fight the right battle, not the most cinematic one.

Dr Simon Nieder

Chesterfield, Derbyshire

Letters, 26 August) reminds us that the Serbelloni group, led by the author’s father, Donald Michie (when he was at Edinburgh University), was weighing the social dangers of artificial intelligence as long ago as 1972. Nor is AI technology itself new, since its roots run back through to Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron of 1957, to the Dartmouth workshop of 1956, and to Alan Turing before that. What is new is that we now have the hardware and software infrastructures to drive it forward at what can sometimes seem to be a terrifying speed.

The Lighthill report of 1973 duly delivered an AI winter in the UK, and the field’s centre of gravity crossed the Atlantic, with the consequences that we all now live with. Donald Michie had worked alongside Turing at Bletchley Park and argued forcefully against the cuts, in the televised Lighthill debate that followed the report, to no avail. The quip attributed to him, perhaps apocryphally, “Let there be Lighthill. And there was darkness”, still resonates strongly in our country today.

As a double-hatted academic (computer scientist and humanities scholar), I would argue for the return of a “Serbelloni debate” that, as Jonathan Michie observes and as his father recognised, requires the involvement of both the sciences and the humanities.

Dr Anthony Harris

Emmanuel College, Cambridge

I worked at OpenAI. Here are the guardrails we need now, 21 August), Miles Brundage failed to mention an international effort seeking broad political support for a global AI treaty. This effort is carrying forward a compelling address at the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva last month, where the secretary general called for human control of AI as its applications spread in weaponry and subversive, prejudicial public surveillance

A fragmented approach, as described by Mr Brundage, is likely to greatly increase the difficulty of implementing AI controls that are timely, internationally negotiated, and therefore effective.

AI, corporate agendas, diverse national defence and economic goals, and the proliferation of energy-intensive datacentres are entangled in interlocking systemic interrelationships that cannot be resolved through disjointed incrementalism. This is especially true as the pace of innovation accelerates, exacerbating worst-case scenarios of advanced AI technology, posing increasingly dire risks.

No matter how well intended, fragmented efforts will be diversionary and cause crucial delays, impeding the diligent pursuit of a systemic global strategy to pre-empt destructive outcomes. Such outcomes could result from malicious use of AI by humans and/or subversive and deceptive activities of renegade algorithms – examples of which are already alarming.

Another troubling aspect of this systemic dilemma must be addressed. Mounting bipartisan opposition to datacentres – well-justified and well-substantiated – is diverting the political attention needed to control AI and implement appropriate restraints (bans or moratoriums) until reliable AI safeguards can be established. This is analogous to focusing on treating a serious symptom in lieu of urgently seeking a remedy for the critical disease that’s causing it. Surely it’s possible to employ a multifaceted strategy, recognising that the sooner rigorous AI guardrails are established, the fewer datacentre harms will be suffered.

Like climate change, the threats of advanced AI are inherently global, making an international approach essential.

David Kyler

Saint Simons Island, Georgia, US

Source 1
Publisher: La Revue française de Généalogie

Original headline: Généatique, du ZX81 à l’intelligence artificielle
English normalization: From the ZX81 to Artificial Intelligence
Evidence basis: full_text
Source evidence: Généatique, du ZX81 à l’intelligence artificielle

Né au milieu des années 1980 dans une maison familiale du Val-d’Oise, Généatique accompagne depuis quarante ans les mutations de la généalogie informatique. Une aventure commencée avec un ZX81 et qui se poursuit aujourd’hui avec l’intelligence artificielle. L’histoire de Généatique commence à Noël 1981, bien avant qu’Internet ne bouleverse la recherche généalogique. À Bessancourt, dans le Val-d’Oise, Lucien Lerebourg, ingénieur en électronique, achète un ZX81 Sinclair doté de 1 ko de mémoire vive. L’ordinateur est livré en kit. Il faut l’assembler, lui ajouter un clavier et de la mémoire. Ses fils participent à l’aventure. L’aîné, François, se passionne pour la programmation.

Quelques années plus tard, Lucien anime avec lui un club informatique à la MJC. En 1986, une discussion avec un adhérent généalogiste donne à François Lerebourg, alors âgé de 18 ans, l’idée de concevoir un programme destiné à enregistrer et imprimer des généalogies. Il se prend lui-même au jeu. Avec ses parents et son frère Philippe, il recherche ses ancêtres, dépouille les actes reçus des mairies et adhère à plusieurs cercles généalogiques.

Les premiers arbres sont rudimentaires. Une imprimante permet de sortir des tableaux sur du papier continu, mais sans traits ni cases. Un gabarit est alors superposé à l’impression. Présenté lors d’une exposition généalogique, le système attire l’attention. Le bouche à oreille se prolonge sur le Minitel, notamment par le 3615 GENEAL, et apporte une première centaine de commandes.

L’entreprise s’organise autour de la maison familiale. François programme dans sa chambre, une secrétaire s’installe sur le palier, puis le garage accueille les premiers salariés. L’Association pour le développement de l’informatique personnelle, ADIP, diffuse le logiciel Généatique sur des disquettes souples de 5 pouces ¼. L’assistance technique est tout aussi artisanale. En vacances, François et son frère rappellent les utilisateurs depuis les cabines téléphoniques des campings.

En 1993, l’association devient une société commerciale, le CDIP. Généatique passe sous Windows dès 1994. La famille sillonne alors les salons avec ordinateurs et écrans pour présenter un logiciel qui s’enrichit régulièrement. Le CDIP diversifie ensuite ses activités avec des logiciels de dépouillement, des cartes de Cassini sur cédérom, le site Guide-Genealogie.com, Photos de Famille ou encore Studio-Scrap. Aujourd'hui, le premier programme de François Lerebourg, Généatique est toujours développé par le CDIP. Le logiciel s’est prolongé sur le Web et les appareils mobiles, tout en conservant sa fonction première, construire, documenter et représenter un arbre généalogique. En 2026, une version native pour Mac a notamment été proposée.

Le nouveau virage est désormais celui de l’intelligence artificielle. Généatique propose des outils de transcription automatique de documents anciens et de traduction des actes. Le logiciel s’appuie également sur les données du projet SOCFACE, qui utilise l’IA pour lire et indexer les recensements nominatifs français. Quarante ans après avoir tenté de faire entrer un arbre généalogique dans quelques kilo-octets, François Lerebourg continue ainsi inlassablement d’explorer ce que l’informatique peut apporter aux généalogistes. Avec là encore, la fidélité d'une communauté soudée autour de son outil.

Le 31 août à 07h07

L’IA générative peut-elle devenir un service public ? La Corée du Sud s’apprête à répondre à cette question. Le pays va en effet proposer aux citoyens un accès gratuit à des services d’IA, avec la promesse de tokens illimités. Un moyen pour Séoul d’atteindre la « souveraineté IA » face aux États-Unis et à la Chine.

En Corée du Sud, l’IA générative bientôt érigée en service public

L’IA générative peut-elle devenir un service public ? La Corée du Sud s’apprête à répondre à cette question. Le pays va en effet proposer aux citoyens un accès gratuit à des services d’IA, avec la promesse de tokens illimités. Un moyen pour Séoul d’atteindre la « souveraineté IA » face aux États-Unis et à la Chine.

Un chatbot gratuit pour chaque citoyen. C’est une des mesures mises en œuvre par le gouvernement coréen, dans le cadre d’un programme plus vaste pour casser la dépendance du pays aux modèles américains et chinois, comme l’explique le Wall Street Journal. Les bots auront des fonctionnalités d’IA classiques, mais ils devront aussi permettre aux utilisateurs de prendre un rendez-vous chez le médecin, recevoir des petites annonces immobilières pour ceux qui veulent déménager, ou obtenir des conseils financiers.

Une IA gratuite, illimitée et souveraine

Les bots donneront aussi aux parents des conseils de contenus éducatifs pour leurs marmots. Les petites entreprises pourront calculer leurs impôts et vérifier leur admissibilité à des programmes d’aide. Ces IA seront en effet connectées aux plateformes gouvernementales, ce qui leur permettra de remplir un rôle de service public, en quelque sorte. Les utilisateurs bénéficieront par ailleurs d’un usage illimité de l’IA.

Séoul a sélectionné trois consortiums, emmenés par les opérateurs télécoms SK Telecom et KT, ainsi que le groupe tech Kakao, éditeur de l’app à tout faire KakaoTalk (elle fait office de messagerie, de réservation de VTC, de gestion bancaire, etc.). Ils n’auront pas le temps de souffler : les premiers bêta-tests auront lieu dès le mois de septembre, avec un déploiement grand public avant la fin de l’année.

Ces trois consortiums recevront un gros coup de pouce de la part de l’État : jusqu’à 512 puces B200 de NVIDIA à se partager. L’État aidera aussi aux coûts de service à partir de l’année prochaine. Chaque acteur prévoit de livrer une application permettant d’accéder à leur chatbot, tout en intégrant cette « IA publique » dans leurs propres outils pour qu’elle soit accessible à un maximum d’utilisateurs. Plus de 20 millions de Coréens utilisent une version gratuite d’un bot IA.

Cette initiative « AI pour tous » fait partie d’un projet plus large visant à développer une « IA souveraine » en Corée du Sud. « À l’ère de l’intelligence artificielle, prendre un jour de retard pourrait signifier prendre une génération entière de retard », déclarait en novembre dernier le président sud-coréen Lee Jae-myung. « Nous faisons actuellement face à une crise urgente, une question de vie ou de mort », soutenait-il devant des parlementaires.

Une question de « survie »

« Seule une course contre la montre nous permettra de survivre. Nous devons sécuriser les éléments fondamentaux de l’intelligence artificielle plus rapidement que n’importe quel autre pays. Les semi-conducteurs, l’IA physique et les centres de données d’IA constituent les trois piliers d’un grand bond en avant. », a-t-il redit fin juin, au moment d’annoncer un gigantesque plan d’investissements dans les usines dédiées à la fabrication de mémoire vive.

Le pays va bâtir des infrastructures, des technologies (puces, LLM) et développer des compétences nationales pour réduire sa dépendance aux modèles étrangers. Le budget de ce programme représente l’équivalent de 6,8 milliards de dollars pour 2026. Un modèle suivi de près par d’autres pays qui ne veulent pas non plus se reposer entièrement sur des systèmes américains ou chinois.

Source 1
Publisher: Lowy Institute

Original headline: Losing face? Licensing and governing AI content in China
English normalization: Losing face? Licensing and governing AI content in China
Evidence basis: full_text
Source evidence: Subscribe to The Informer for monthly expert analysis, and to Events for advance notice of visiting world leaders and distinguished guests.

The most-pressing world events explained by Lowy Institute experts and global contributors, in your inbox, every Thursday.

A staff member works on script refinement, on-location filming, AI post-production, and overseas translation and distribution at a micro drama production company on 21 July 2026 in Jiaxing, China (VCG via Getty Images)

A face licensed for one AI advert can be reused indefinitely, and local laws have not caught up with that.

Would you accept US$15 to let an AI company use your face in artificial intelligence generated content?

In China, this is becoming a real proposition. A recent Rest of World (Opens in new window) article reports that people are paid from between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses for AI-generated microdramas and advertisements produced for mobile phone viewing.

China’s mobile entertainment industry is already enormous – and the use of AI-generated content is growing. More than 95% of microdramas released in China during the first three months of 2026 reportedly used AI somewhere in their production. The industry needs more faces – celebrities and ordinary people – to meet the demand for fast-paced, audience-driven microdrama production (Opens in new window).

One response has been straightforward: pay people for their faces.

At the same time, regulators and platforms are cracking down on harmful and pirated content (Opens in new window),unauthorised digital likeness (Opens in new window), and homogeneous AI-generated characters.

Licensing might be “legal” rather than simply scraping somebody’s photographs or reproducing their likeness without permission. But it creates a new problem for AI governance. An agreement might authorise one advertisement. But could the same AI facial model later appear in 100 advertisements? A romance or a political drama? Could it be aged, sexualised or made to say things you would never say?

Generative AI transforms the question of facial rights. It is no longer only about protecting people from having their identity stolen. It is about governing what an authorised digital likeness can be made to do – potentially forever.

Who controls the image? (Wang Gang/China News Service/VCG via Getty Images)

A face can now operate simultaneously in at least three ways.

It remains a social identity, through which people recognise one another and negotiate reputation, recognition and belonging.

In Chinese history, the face has been understood through social relationships, to capture ideas of reputation, dignity, recognition and social standing. To “lose face” traditionally means (Opens in new window) to suffer a loss of status or social standing in the eyes of others.

In the digital era, the face has become a biometric identifier. Facial recognition presents a difficult governance challenge, requiring adaptive policy (Opens in new window) response to disruptive technologies and changing citizen expectations (Opens in new window). It turns physical appearance into machine-readable information that can authenticate a payment, unlock a device, verify an identity for transaction or access to a physical space, and trigger surveillance networks in population management.

Generative AI is now turning the face into something else: a reproducible digital asset.

Facial recognition is primarily concerned with identification, “who is this person?” Generative AI asks, “what can this face do?” The face is detachable from the body, reusable across time and space, through which different stories and formats can be produced for different audiences across platforms. This raises questions about consent and ownership when a face can be licensed for AI generative images.

Who shares in the ongoing value – and who bears the reputational cost – of an indefinitely productive likeness.

China already has substantial laws governing faces. Under the Civil Code, portrait rights form part of a person’s broader personality rights. Individuals have rights over the production, use and publication of their likeness, while unauthorised fabrication or misuse through information technology can constitute an infringement.

Biometric information is also treated as sensitive personal information under China’s personal information protection regime. The 2025 Measures on the Security Management of Facial Recognition Technology Applications (Opens in new window), which came into force on 1 June 2025, define facial information as biometric information associated with an identified or identifiable natural person and establish requirements for the processing and protection of such information.

China also regulates generative AI. The Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (Opens in new window), effective since August 2023, cover generative services producing text, images, audio and video and explicitly connect AI governance with personal information, data security and the protection of individual rights.

Yet China’s emerging facial economy raises a governance question that goes beyond privacy and rights. It is also about value: when a face becomes a reusable AI asset, its value is not exhausted by the initial licensing fee. A modest one-off payment may enable repeated commercial use across advertisements, dramas and platforms, while the resulting value rests with AI firms, studios and distributors.

The question is therefore not only whether a person consented, but who shares in the ongoing value – and who bears the reputational cost – of an indefinitely productive likeness.

Licensing could offer people greater control over their likeness. But consent is not the end of the story. It should not become a one-time transaction for an indefinitely reproducible facial identity whose future uses cannot be anticipated.

This challenge cuts across portrait and personality rights, data protection, contract law, labour and the distribution of economic value. A meaningful licensing framework should specify permitted uses, duration and scope. It should also prohibit sensitive uses, enable traceability, and consider whether continued commercial use requires renewed consent or further payment.

The challenge for licensing and governing the face is not simply to prevent identity theft. It is to determine how real human faces can be governed when they become raw material for synthetic worlds, from consent to taking control over where they go, what they do, and what value they generate.

August 5, 2026

Par: National Committee Against Smoking

Dernière mise à jour: August 31, 2026

Temps de lecture: 6 minutes

In July 2026, tobacco company Philip Morris International (PMI) announced the establishment of a "generative artificial intelligence factory" at its Portuguese subsidiary, Tabaqueira, in Albarraque. Presented as a global center of excellence, this facility is expected to employ up to one hundred specialists and serve all of the group's activities, from optimizing industrial processes to developing new AI-based applications. In parallel, the company's global communications director detailed, in an interview published in August 2026, how the group is reorienting its corporate communications to become more accessible to major language models, notably by using artificial audience "personas" and optimizing its corporate website for generative search engines.

These announcements come a few weeks after the STOP monitoring network issued a warning about the tobacco industry's use of artificial intelligence to influence public discourse on its products. They illustrate how tobacco companies can leverage these tools, both as an industrial tool and as an instrument for influencing the information available on tobacco and nicotine.

A generative AI "factory" installed at the group's Portuguese subsidiary

According to the Portuguese Agency for Investment and Foreign Trade (AICEP), PMI chose Portugal to establish its "GenAI Factory", housed in the Tabaqueira facilities in Albarraque[1]-[2]. The site is described as a global center of excellence responsible for developing and deploying generative artificial intelligence solutions for all of the group's operational units.

The announced uses cover the optimization of industrial processes, data analysis, automation of operations, and the creation of new AI-powered applications. This expansion builds on the group's long-standing presence in Portugal, where Tabaqueira also houses a technology center and a financial center. According to AICEP, 26 of Tabaqueira's employees now hold positions with global reach. The corporate communications accompanying the announcement highlight cooperation with Portuguese universities, research centers, and companies, as well as the training of highly qualified personnel, positioning the operation as a contribution to the national innovation ecosystem.

Corporate communication explicitly calibrated for language models

In an interview with Business Insider, published in August 2026[3], Moira Gilchrist, PMI's global communications director, described how the group's communications strategy has adapted to the rise of generative AI tools. She presented herself as an early and committed user of these technologies.

Two developments are highlighted. The first involves building artificial audience "personas," that is, simulated profiles used to test the resonance of messages before their dissemination—feedback presented as a way to improve the group's communication. The second concerns the company's institutional website: according to Moira Gilchrist, it has become «"an important vector for restoring the facts, because major language models access information.". The group states that it has shifted its efforts from optimization for traditional search engines to optimization for generative engines, structuring its content so that it is picked up by conversational systems.

This interview is part of the transformation narrative that the group has been deploying for several years around its so-called "smoke-free" products, which accounted for 43% of its net sales in the first quarter of 2026. This transformation narrative, widely documented by public health literature as a central element of the industry's repositioning strategy, constitutes precisely the message that these devices aim to make accessible to AI systems.

An ability to influence discourse already noted by public health experts

These announcements echo the alert published at the end of June 2026 by STOP[4], global tobacco industry monitoring network. This work documented manufacturers' use of artificial intelligence to gain public trust and influence online opinion, through both overt and covert means.

Two main mechanisms have been identified. The first is based on volume: by multiplying content favorable to its products on social networks and video platforms, the industry increases the likelihood that this content will be picked up by search engines and chatbots, which build their responses based on what is most prevalent online. The second relates to the age of the available material: industry-funded studies and advertorials broadcast over several decades remain accessible on the web and continue to feed the data on which these systems rely, without their origin necessarily being disclosed to the user.

STOP also highlighted the risk of coordinated or automated campaigns disrupting monitoring tools and public consultations, as well as the development of an AI model designed specifically for the sector.

The issue lies less in the tool itself than in the channel. By explicitly optimizing its corporate content for use by chatbots, a tobacco manufacturer seeks to position itself upstream of the responses delivered to users, including healthcare professionals, journalists, and public officials, without revealing the industrial origin of the message. Public health stakeholders point out that this risk has already been demonstrated in consultation processes. In June 2026, an investigation by Dutch public media revealed that Philip Morris International had made available an AI tool that generated approximately 22,500 of the 88,000 contributions to the European consultation on the revision of the tobacco control directives.[5]. In the United States, a study shows that 97 of the 246,808 comments sent to the FDA regarding the menthol ban were form letters, 46 of which contained content attributable to tobacco companies.[6]. This type of interposition is what Article 5.3 of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control targets.
